summary: Texas does not regulate keeping, breeding, or selling pet roof rats at the state level, now confirmed in writing by TPWD (June 2026): as a non-native exotic rodent, Rattus rattus falls outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (indigenous species only), the 'dangerous wild animal' law, and TAHC's 'exotic livestock' (hooved-animal) entry rules. A retail storefront still needs the local city's pet-shop license, wholesale/sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing, and international movement is federally restricted (roof rats are 'wildlife'). Releasing one is illegal.
agency_confirmations: Texas Parks & Wildlife Department (Wildlife Permits Office), written reply June 2026: because roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not native to Texas, no TPWD permit is required to keep them. All TPWD permits regulate the possession, transport, and display of native/indigenous species only, so a non-native roof rat is entirely outside TPWD's permit scope.

keep.why: Texas regulates exotic-pet possession by banning specific hazardous species, not by a permit list. Rattus rattus is a non-native rodent, so it is outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (which cover only species INDIGENOUS to Texas, TPWC §67.001) and is not a listed 'dangerous wild animal' (Health & Safety Code ch. 822). No state possession permit is required. (Local ordinances may cap how many pets a household may keep.)
keep.governing_law: Tex. Parks & Wildlife Code §67.001 (nongame = indigenous); Tex. Health & Safety Code ch. 822 (dangerous wild animals, not rats).

breed.why: There is no Texas breeder license for rodents, the Dog or Cat Breeders Act (Occupations Code ch. 802) covers only dogs and cats. Hobby and commercial rat breeding are unregulated by the state. (Federal USDA licensing still applies to WHOLESALE or sight-unseen sales, see United States.)
breed.governing_law: Tex. Occupations Code ch. 802 (Dog or Cat Breeders Act, dogs/cats only).

sell_give.why: Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated by the state: the TPWD Commercial Nongame Dealer permit applies only to INDIGENOUS wildlife (31 TAC §65.325), so it doesn't cover non-native rats. Two layers still apply: a retail storefront needs the local city's pet-shop license, and wholesale or sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing (see United States).
sell_give.governing_law: 31 Tex. Admin. Code §65.325 (commercial nongame = indigenous); local municipal pet-shop ordinances.

transport.why: Within Texas and across state lines, no state permit or health certificate is required for pet rats: rodents are exempt from TAHC's 'exotic livestock' entry rules (those cover hooved animals) and from the DSHS rabies transport ban (rodents are low-risk). Airlines typically require a vet health certificate to fly. International import/export is restricted at the FEDERAL level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban), see United States.
transport.governing_law: Tex. Agric. Code §142.001 / 4 TAC ch. 51 (exotic livestock = ungulates, excludes rodents); 25 TAC §169 (rabies transport ban, not rodents).

restrictions.summary: A retail pet-store storefront needs the local city's Pet Shop License / commercial animal establishment permit (sanitation, zoning, records). Rules vary by municipality (Houston, Austin, Dallas, etc.). Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways do not need a state license.
steps: Check your city's animal-establishment / pet-shop licensing if running a storefront
restrictions.where_to_file: Your city's animal control / code enforcement

restrictions.summary: Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is illegal in Texas, it is criminal abandonment under the animal-cruelty law (Penal Code §42.092), and they are an invasive non-native species. Rehome responsibly (shelter, rescue, or new owner); never release.

inquiry_focus: We want to confirm that Texas requires no state permit, license, or health certificate to keep, breed, or sell captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus), and whether any CVI/entry requirement applies to bringing them into Texas (TAHC appears to exempt rodents from its 'exotic livestock' entry rules).
